rows.title: INTRODUCTION TO FINANCIAL PLANNING
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Students completing this course satisfactorily will be able to:
outcomes: Use time and value of money concepts to develop money management strategies, plan personal finances, and create a tax strategy.
Understand concepts for making a budget, choosing investments, and purchasing life insurance in order to manage personal finances.
Integrate investment decisions with retirement and estate planning considerations to support long-term financial stability.
objectives: Analyze financial instruments and prepare a short- and long-term financial plan and financial goals for the purpose of creating psychological and emotional well being and security.
Critique the major aspects of current financial systems, markets, and institutions and how they operate in order to achieve intellectual insight as to how they affect our sociological knowledge.

Analyze investments in terms of income tax regulations, retirement, and estate planning for the purpose of long-term stability and social development with respect to various economic and financial implications.
Evaluate the following major financial instruments in terms of understanding risk as related to human perception and their behavioral consequences. a. Insurance b. Stocks and bonds c. Real Estate
Make informed home and auto ownership decisions.

rows.title: CERAMICS - HANDBUILDING I
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Students completing this course satisfactorily will be able to:
outcomes: Create a written project proposal citing historical and/or cultural influences and implement it in clay.
Correctly identify construction methods and decorative techniques along with how these techniques have been used historically and their cultural significance.

Create a body of work utilizing the basic skills needed for handbuilding (pinch, hard slab, soft slab, coil, mold making, slip casting), decorative techniques (sgraffito, marbling, slip trailing, wax resit, glazing) and variety of firing temps and atmospheres (low fire, high fire, raku, oxidation, reduction) that is free of obvious flaws such as cracks or glaze drips.
objectives: Differentiate clay varieties and ceramic handbuilding processes
Create ceramic forms utilizing pinch, coil, soft slab, hard slab techniques
Analyze and demonstrate existing ceramic pieces and distinguish the forming processes used in creating them throughout history
Produce and apply surface treatment to a variety of different forms
Create and utilize one piece molds
Examine and describe historical and contemporary developments, trends, materials, and approaches in ceramics
Create and implement project proposals
Assess and critique ceramics in group, individual, and written contexts using relevant critique formats, concepts and terminology
Safely handle and use all studio equipment, tools, and materials

rows.title: ELEMENTARY CHINESE
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Students completing this course satisfactorily will be able to:
outcomes: Demonstrate an appreciation of the culture, including formative historical events and relevant geographical information.
Demonstrate in writing, proficiency in the use of grammatical structures presented and vocabulary assigned to produce simple sentences and high-frequency characters.
Demonstrate orally, proficiency in the use of the grammatical structures presented and vocabulary assigned to communicate basic personal information and immediate needs.
objectives: Comprehend native daily spoken Chinese in selected social situations.
Communicate in selected social situations.
Recognize and utilize basic grammatical structures.
Comprehend reading of selected written passages in Chinese.
Compose original sentences that incorporate the material acquired through reading and speaking activities.
Identify an additional 400 vocabulary words and relate them to selected social situations.
Identify, select, and give examples of appropriate social levels of speech.
Compare and contrast general aspects of culture and daily life of Chinese speaking population with that of students.
Develop appreciation for historic, political and artistic individuals.
Use software appropriate to the material being taught.
Generate solutions to a variety of problems and exercises dealing with vocabulary expressions, grammar, pronunciation, listening, speaking, reading and writing.

rows.title: ELECTRONICS FOR COMPUTER TECHNOLOGISTS
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Students completing this course satisfactorily will be able to:
outcomes: List and describe common devices and techniques to protect computer hardware.
Write the electronic definition and the unit of measure for common DC and AC electronic quantities.
Convert a decimal number to binary.
Calculate the proper wattage rating for a computer power supply.
Write the schematic symbol and electronic function of common semiconductor devices.
Determine the performance of a series and/or parallel circuit
Determine the RMS voltage and frequency of an oscilloscope display of a sinewave.
objectives: Define and describe basic electronic DC and AC quantities - current, voltage, power, resistance, capacitance, inductance, frequency, period, others.

Describe the function and operation of basic DC and AC electronic components - resistors, capacitors, inductors, transformers, semiconductors, combinational logic devices, sequential logic devices, memory devices, others.
Describe general troubleshooting techniques for electronics and computers.
List and describe devices and techniques to protect computer hardware.
List the main functions of and controls for an oscilloscope, power supply, and digital multimeter.
List the main electronic components in computer power supplies and perform calculations to properly determine the wattage ratings for computer supplies.

rows.title: DANCE PRODUCTION
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Students completing this course satisfactorily will be able to:
outcomes: Students will view and select dancers for technical strength, dance comprehension, alignment and performance quality.
Students will write a critique reflecting their creative and performance process during the semester.
Students will demonstrate proficiency by rehearsing and performing choreography in various dance techniques.
Students will stage dances for a concert performance with technical support in lighting and music while choosing appropriate costume and make-up for this venue.
Students will display a knowledge of theatrical vocabulary and terminology through the preparation of dance choreography.
objectives: Identify choreographic elements of dance
Identify technical support in staging dance
Demonstrate self-expression through dance performance
Demonstrate cooperation through group interaction and discipline
Complete an assessment of the production process

rows.title: INTRODUCTION TO ETHNIC STUDIES
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Students completing this course satisfactorily will be able to:
outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to explain anti-racist and anti-colonial issues as articulated by Native American, African American, Asian American, and Chicanx and Latinx activists and social movements.

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to apply concepts of Ethnic Studies such as race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethnocentrism, Eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, imperialism, settler colonialism, and anti-racism.

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to analyze the intersection of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, ability, tribal citizenship, sovereignty, language, and/or age in Native American. African American, Asian American, and Chicanx and Latinx communities.

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to explain the critical events, histories, cultures, intellectual traditions, contributions, lived-experiences, and social struggles of Native American, African American, Asian American, and Chicanx and Latinx communities.

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to identify how Native American, African American, Asian American, and Chicanx and Latinx struggles for racial and social justice are relevant to current and structural issues.

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to discuss theory and knowledge produced by Native Americans African Americans, Asian Americans, and/or Chicanx and Latinx individuals.
objectives: Analyze and articulate concepts such as race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethno-centrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, imperialism, settler colonialism, and anti-racism as analyzed by Ethnic Studies, Native American Studies, African American Studies, Asian American Studies, and/or Latina and Latino American Studies.

Apply theory and knowledge produced by Native American, African American, Asian American, and/or Latina and Latino American communities to describe the critical events, histories, cultures, intellectual traditions, contributions, lived-experiences, and social struggles of those groups with a particular emphasis on agency and group-affirmation.

Critically analyze the intersection of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, tribal citizenship, sovereignty, language, and/or age in Native American, African American, Asian American, and/or Latina or Latino American communities.

Critically review how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and enacted by Native Americans, African Americans, Asian Americans and/or Latina and Latino Americans, are relevant to current and structural issues such as communal, national, international, and transnational politics as, for example, in immigration, reparations, settler-colonialism, multiculturalism, and language policies.

Describe and actively engage with anti-racist and anti-colonial issues and the practices and movements in Native American, African American, Asian American, and/or Latina and Latino American communities to build a just and equitable society.

outcomes: Analyze and evaluate animated works in terms of style, technical merit, and historical significance.
Identify and evaluate cultural and societal perspectives in animated works.
Identify the major technological developments of animated media.
objectives: Define and identify the use of animation as a medium for communication, education, and entertainment.
Discuss and analyze the key historical developments in animation.
Identify the major technological developments of animated media.
Analyze and evaluate animated works in terms of style, technical merit, and historical significance.
Identify and evaluate cultural and societal perspectives in animated works.

rows.title: RACE, ETHNICITY, AND RESISTANCE IN THE U.S.
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Students completing this course satisfactorily will be able to:
outcomes: Apply concepts of Ethnic Studies such as race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethnocentrism, Eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, imperialism, settler colonialism, and anti-racism.
Discuss theory and knowledge produced by Native Americans African Americans, Asian Americans, and/or Chicanx and Latinx individuals.

Explain the critical events, histories, cultures, intellectual traditions, contributions, lived-experiences, and social struggles of Native American, African American, Asian American, and Chicanx and Latinx.

Analyze the intersection of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, ability, tribal citizenship, sovereignty, language, and/or age in Native American. African American, Asian American, and Chicanx and Latinx communities.
Identify how Native American, African American, Asian American, and Chicanx and Latinx struggles for racial and social justice are relevant to current and structural issues.
Explain anti-racist and anti-colonial issues as articulated by Native American, African American, Asian American, and Chicanx and Latinx activists and social movements.
objectives: Analyze and evaluate the histories of migration, colonialization, diaspora, social justice and racialization of core racialized groups in the United States—African American, Native American, Asian American, and Chicanx/Latinx people—and its impact on ethnic and racial formations in the US.
Assess and explain the historical roots and contemporary consequences of institutional racism, racial stereotypes, segregation, discrimination, and prejudice in U.S. history.

Describe the histories, cultures, intellectual traditions, and contributions; struggles for self-determination and agency; group-affirmation epistemologies; and methodology of African Americans, Native Americans, Asian Americans, and Chicanx/Latinx to explain and analyze lived experiences, events, history, and social struggles.

Identify and explain key concepts such as racism, eurocentrism, liberation, settler colonialism, anti-racism, and equity, as well as theories, methodologies, and policy related to African Americans, Native Americans, Asian Americans, and Chicanx/Latinx using an intersectional lens that includes race, class, gender, sexuality, age, religion, national origin, ability, and/or language.

Analyze and articulate the cultural production, exchanges, theories and ways of knowing of African Americans, Native Americans, Asian Americans, and Chicanx/Latinx to explain discrimination and promote anti-racist and social justice practices to build a just and equitable world.

Critically analyze and describe anti-racist, anti-colonial, and anti-imperialist issues and movements in African American, Native American, Asian American, and Chicanx/Latinx communities that are relevant to current and structural issues.

rows.title: FUNDAMENTALS OF INTERIOR DESIGN
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Students completing this course satisfactorily will be able to:
outcomes: Aesthetically combine color, texture and pattern in the coordination of materials and products used in living environments.
Define the Elements & Principles of Interior Design for interior environments.
Demonstrate knowledge of floor plans in relation to space planning and furniture arrangement in a design project.
objectives: Explain the role human factors and behavioral sciences play in the design of interior environments to address the social, physical, and psychological needs of occupants of different ages and abilities.
Identify and analyze the elements and principles of design in interior spaces.

Demonstrate knowledge of color theories and applications in design and understanding of color-related psychological, physiological, environmental, and cultural factors which affect human environments.

Discuss interior construction and building systems such as mechanical, electrical, plumbing, acoustical in relation to their impact on the design of interiors and the health, safety, and welfare of the occupants.
Analyze floor plans and furniture arrangements in relation to residential space planning, universal design principles, and meeting human needs for a sense of place and cultural sensitivity.
Evaluate lighting and lighting systems in interiors and the psychological and physiological effect of light on human behavior and well-being.

Compare and contrast various types of furnishings, fixtures, finish materials, textiles, and accessories - including sustainable and innovative materials - regarding function, aesthetics, ecology, and wellness.
Select and aesthetically combine color, texture, and pattern to coordinate materials and products used for living environments.
Analyze cultural and historical influences and adaptations as they affect human environments and a diversity of lifestyles.
Assess sustainable and biophilic design practices as they relate to environmental and ecological issues.

Demonstrate knowledge of the design process to identify a range of problems and generate creative solutions that address the complex physical, mental, and emotional needs of people within the interior environment.

rows.title: BASIC INFORMATION COMPETENCY SKILLS, LIBRARY RESEARCH
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Students completing this course satisfactorily will be able to:
outcomes: Students will be able to demonstrate ability to be able to properly format a citation.
Students will be able to demonstrate ability to select resources for research based upon authority, credibility and relevance.
Students will be able to demonstrate ability to articulate a topic for research that is flexible and adaptable.
objectives: Locate, use and evaluate print and/or electronic resources in an academic library.
Apply research and critical thinking skills to organize, synthesize, and evaluate information.
Retrieve and utilize information from the Library Online Catalog and subscription online databases.
Prepare a "works cited" list of information sources using the MLA or APA documentation style.
Apply information-seeking strategies in other libraries.

rows.title: INTRODUCTION TO PUBLIC HEALTH
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Students completing this course satisfactorily will be able to:
outcomes: Describe an event that transformed public health.
Identify occupational hazards and their prevention measures.
Identify the components of the Whole School, Whole Child, Whole Community (WSCC) model.
objectives: Define important foundational concepts in community/public health.
Distinguish the difference between personal and public health.
Identify different public health disciplines, professions and organizations, and explain how each contributes to the field of public health.
Describe the historical achievements of public health and their impact today.
Demonstrate the use of basic epidemiological methods, such as the analysis of rates, and the definition of cases, population at risk, risk factors, incidence, prevalence, morbidity and mortality.
Outline strategies for prevention, detection and control of infectious and chronic disease.
Identify the components of the Whole School, Whole Child, Whole Community (WSCC) model designed to improve learning and health in our nation’s schools.
Outline the process of community organizing, building and health promotion programming.
Analyze current public health issues and describe how they affect societal well-being among specific populations of age, sex, ethnicity, minority, education and socioeconomic status.
Describe the Dual Diagnosis/Co-Occurring Disorders approach to treating people who suffer from both an addiction and a psychiatric disorder.

Describe the interplay between health determinants, such as environmental conditions, social, behavioral and cultural factors, and biological considerations, and explain the role of each in determining local, national and global health organization and policy.
Analyze the organization, financing and delivery of various medical and population-based services in the U.S. healthcare system.
Distinguish how public health differs from the traditional Western medicine approach to treating disease and illness.
Describe the inter-relationship between human beings and their environment and public health initiatives and policies to protect the planet.
Identify common practices that contribute to intentional and unintentional workplace injuries and public health policies that would reduce their occurrences.
Communicate orally and in writing in the scientific language of the discipline.
Interpret and evaluate public health and medical information from general and subject specific library and credible Internet sources.

rows.title: HONORS POLITICAL THEORY
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Students completing this course satisfactorily will be able to:
outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course students will demonstrate an understanding and critical analysis of Plato’s, Republic or Aristotle’s, Politics.
Demonstrate an understanding and critical analysis of Plato’s, Republic or Aristotle’s, Politics.
Demonstrate an understanding and critical analysis of Niccolo Machiavelli’s, The Prince.
Demonstrate an understanding and critical analysis of John Stuart Mill’s, On Liberty.
Demonstrate an understanding and critical analysis of Karl Marx’s The Communist Manifesto.
Demonstrate an understanding and critical analysis of John Locke’s Second Treatise on Government.
objectives: Analyze selected works in political theory, including but not limited to the works of Plato, John Locke, Karl Marx, John Stuart Mill, and other major political theorists.
Compare the social and economic forces that have affected the outlooks of these selected political thinkers.
Trace the continuity in the lineage of political theory from ancient to modern times.
Refer to historical issues as an aid in understanding contemporary issues.
